groups.title: Inversion of control
groups.mechanism: The container manages bean creation and dependency resolution from definitions. Application code should express collaborators while retaining responsibility for domain invariants.
groups.tradeOff: Container integration improves composition but should not make business logic require a running context.
groups.verify: Construct the domain service directly in one test and exercise its container wiring in another.

questions.question: What is inversion of control in Spring?
questions.answer: The container controls construction and wiring of configured objects, rather than application components manually locating and assembling all collaborators.

questions.question: How does dependency injection support testing?
questions.answer: A service can receive a controlled collaborator through its constructor, allowing its business behavior to be tested without starting Spring.

questions.question: What does ApplicationContext add to BeanFactory?
questions.answer: ApplicationContext combines bean management with application features including events, resources and environment integration; it is the usual application-level container.

questions.question: Why is the service-locator pattern harder to reason about?
questions.answer: Dependencies are discovered inside methods instead of declared at construction, hiding requirements and complicating isolated tests and lifecycle ownership.

questions.question: How would you keep a domain model independent of Spring?
questions.answer: Keep business decisions in ordinary types with explicit dependencies; place container configuration and infrastructure adapters at application boundaries.

groups.title: Constructor injection and cycles
groups.mechanism: Constructor dependencies express required state before an object becomes usable. A cycle signals mutually dependent construction, even when deferred lookup can postpone it.
groups.tradeOff: Lazy resolution can unblock construction while leaving the underlying design cycle intact.
groups.verify: Start a context with missing and cyclic collaborators and verify failure explains the dependency path.

questions.question: Why prefer constructor injection for required dependencies?
questions.answer: It exposes requirements, supports final fields and makes incomplete construction harder. It also enables straightforward unit construction without reflective field injection.

questions.question: When is setter injection reasonable?
questions.answer: For genuinely optional or reconfigurable collaborators with a documented valid default state, rather than as a way to conceal required dependencies.

questions.question: How does Spring resolve a single constructor injection point?
questions.answer: A bean with one constructor can generally use it without Autowired; argument resolution still depends on eligible candidates and qualifiers.

questions.question: Why is Lazy not always a sound circular-dependency fix?
questions.answer: It can defer the failure until use or preserve tangled responsibilities. Refactor shared policy or orchestration when the cycle reflects a design problem.

questions.question: How would you split two services that call each other during construction?
questions.answer: Extract common capabilities or introduce an orchestrator so dependencies form a directed construction graph with explicit runtime collaboration.

groups.title: Bean scopes
groups.mechanism: Singleton scope is one instance per container definition, not one instance per JVM or a thread-safety promise. Scoped collaborators require explicit lifetime handling.
groups.tradeOff: Long-lived sharing reduces construction but increases the importance of state confinement.
groups.verify: Overlap two users and verify no request data leaks through singleton fields.

questions.question: What does Spring singleton scope mean?
questions.answer: The container maintains one shared instance for that bean definition within its context, rather than guaranteeing one object globally across the process.

questions.question: When should prototype scope be used?
questions.answer: For objects requiring a fresh instance on lookup, with a clear ownership and cleanup contract. It does not make every injection dynamically fresh.

questions.question: What happens when a prototype is injected once into a singleton?
questions.answer: The singleton normally retains the particular injected instance. Use a provider or supported scoped mechanism for repeated runtime lookup.

questions.question: Why does a singleton service holding current-user state fail under load?
questions.answer: Requests share the same field and race, potentially mixing identities. Pass request data explicitly or use a correctly managed request scope.

questions.question: How would you manage prototype resources safely?
questions.answer: Define the caller as owner where appropriate and close each created instance explicitly; do not assume the container manages the full destruction lifecycle.

groups.title: Lifecycle callbacks
groups.mechanism: Bean initialization and destruction occur within a container lifecycle. Initialization callbacks are not a substitute for readiness policy or durable job recovery.
groups.tradeOff: Eager initialization finds failures sooner but increases startup dependencies.
groups.verify: Fail initialization, close the context and verify each owned resource is cleaned up without hiding the original error.

questions.question: What is the purpose of PostConstruct?
questions.answer: It runs initialization after dependency injection, allowing a managed bean to validate or prepare state before normal use.

questions.question: When should InitializingBean be avoided in domain code?
questions.answer: Prefer framework-independent initialization or lifecycle annotations when coupling business types directly to Spring's callback interfaces offers no clear benefit.

questions.question: How do bean post-processors relate to initialization?
questions.answer: They participate around bean initialization and can wrap objects, including with proxies; lifecycle behavior depends on the configured processing chain.

questions.question: Why can starting threads in a constructor cause leaks?
questions.answer: Construction can fail before ownership is registered, leaving workers running. Start and stop resources through deliberate lifecycle boundaries.

questions.question: How would you implement orderly application shutdown?
questions.answer: Stop admitting work, wait within a defined deadline, interrupt cooperatively when appropriate and release resources with observable incomplete-work recovery.

groups.title: Qualifiers and candidate selection
groups.mechanism: Type matching can yield several candidates. Qualifiers narrow the desired role; Primary provides a preference where applicable without deleting other definitions.
groups.tradeOff: Implicit defaults reduce wiring but can hide accidental configuration overlap.
groups.verify: Resolve named and unqualified injection points under missing and duplicate candidate configurations.

questions.question: What is the difference between Qualifier and Primary?
questions.answer: Qualifier narrows the intended candidate set; Primary expresses a preferred candidate when multiple eligible single-valued dependencies remain.

questions.question: When should a collection of beans be injected?
questions.answer: When the service deliberately composes all implementations, such as a strategy registry, with explicit ordering and duplicate handling.

questions.question: Does bean registration order define reliable business precedence?
questions.answer: No. Use a documented ordering mechanism or explicit domain priority; incidental scanning or registration order is not a business contract.

questions.question: Why can two primary beans still fail injection?
questions.answer: Primary is a preference mechanism, not a uniqueness constraint that automatically selects between multiple equally preferred candidates.

questions.question: How would you select a tenant-specific strategy safely?
questions.answer: Use validated tenant identity and an explicit allowlisted registry. Reject unknown mappings instead of falling back to an arbitrary implementation.

groups.title: Java configuration
groups.mechanism: Configuration classes register definitions; Bean methods describe managed objects. Full configuration proxying and lite mode have different inter-method-call semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Reducing proxying can simplify AOT and startup but requires explicit collaborator parameters.
groups.verify: Count created instances when one configuration method calls another in both supported modes.

questions.question: What does a Bean method declare?
questions.answer: A recipe for a container-managed object, including its identity and lifecycle metadata; it is more than a general-purpose factory helper.

questions.question: When is Configuration proxyBeanMethods=false suitable?
questions.answer: When configuration methods do not depend on intercepted self-calls to retrieve shared beans; pass required beans as method parameters instead.

questions.question: How does a full Configuration class preserve singleton inter-bean calls?
questions.answer: Its enhanced configuration object can intercept Bean method calls and delegate retrieval to the container.

questions.question: Why can direct calls to lite-mode Bean methods create duplicate clients?
questions.answer: Those calls behave like ordinary Java method calls and can create fresh objects rather than retrieving the managed singleton.

questions.question: How would you review third-party client bean configuration?
questions.answer: Check scope, construction arguments, conditional registration, connection reuse, destruction hooks and whether any direct factory calls bypass the container.

groups.title: Environment and property sources
groups.mechanism: Environment resolves properties from ordered sources and active profiles. Binding and validation are separate from finding a key.
groups.tradeOff: Flexible external configuration requires deterministic precedence and safe diagnostics.
groups.verify: Provide conflicting sources plus missing, blank and invalid values; assert resolved values without printing secrets.

questions.question: What does Spring Environment represent?
questions.answer: The application's active profiles and property-resolution view, allowing code and configuration to inspect environment-dependent values.

questions.question: When should Profile be used?
questions.answer: For deliberate environment-specific bean composition. Avoid scattering business feature decisions across many profile names with unclear combinations.

questions.question: How does property resolution differ from type conversion?
questions.answer: Resolution chooses a value for a key; conversion interprets that value as a required type, which can still fail afterward.

questions.question: Why can a correctly named property have no business effect?
questions.answer: Nothing may bind or read it, or another source may override it. Inspect the actual binding target and effective configuration.

questions.question: How would you change a runtime setting safely?
questions.answer: Define whether beans support refresh, validate the new configuration atomically and specify how in-flight work and old resources transition.

groups.title: AOP and proxy boundaries
groups.mechanism: Spring proxy AOP intercepts calls through the proxy. Advice does not automatically apply to ordinary target self-invocation or manually constructed instances.
groups.tradeOff: Cross-cutting behavior is concise but invocation paths become part of correctness.
groups.verify: Call the same operation externally and through a self-call; observe actual advice execution.

questions.question: What is an aspect in Spring AOP?
questions.answer: A declaration of cross-cutting behavior applied at selected method execution join points through configured advice and pointcuts.

questions.question: When are interface proxies and class proxies appropriate?
questions.answer: Interface proxies expose interfaces; subclass proxies expose a class shape but cannot override final methods. Choose according to actual application contracts.

questions.question: Why does self-invocation bypass ordinary Spring proxy advice?
questions.answer: The target calls itself directly without routing the invocation through the external proxy that owns the interceptor chain.

questions.question: Why might a private Transactional method not establish a transaction?
questions.answer: Private methods cannot be intercepted by normal subclass override, and ordinary proxy calls cannot expose them as external advised methods.

questions.question: How would you combine metrics, retry and transactions?
questions.answer: Specify interceptor ordering and verify attempt counts, transaction boundaries and timing semantics. Outer versus inner advice changes the meaning of measurements and rollback.

groups.title: Transaction boundaries
groups.mechanism: A transaction manager coordinates a specific resource model. Declarative annotations establish logical boundaries whose physical effects depend on propagation and the invocation path.
groups.tradeOff: Wide transactions simplify atomic local work but retain locks and connections longer.
groups.verify: Force failure before commit and inspect durable state from an independent transaction.

questions.question: What does Transactional do?
questions.answer: It supplies transaction metadata used by Spring's transaction infrastructure around eligible managed invocations; the annotation alone does not execute a transaction.

questions.question: Where should a transaction boundary usually live?
questions.answer: Around a coherent service use case that needs atomic local data changes, while keeping slow remote operations outside where practical.

questions.question: Which exceptions trigger default declarative rollback?
questions.answer: Normally unchecked exceptions and Errors trigger rollback; checked exceptions require an explicit rule when rollback is intended. Verify the configured policy.

questions.question: Why can catching an exception still lead to UnexpectedRollbackException?
questions.answer: An inner participating operation may have marked the shared transaction rollback-only; catching its exception does not necessarily clear that state.

questions.question: How would you coordinate a database commit with message publication?
questions.answer: Persist publication intent in the database transaction and relay it durably, or use another explicit protocol. Account for duplicate delivery after relay crashes.

groups.title: Propagation and savepoints
groups.mechanism: Propagation controls how logical invocations interact with transactions. Independent physical transactions and nested savepoints have different resource and recovery semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Independent transactions isolate commits but can consume additional connections and violate all-or-nothing expectations.
groups.verify: Observe committed rows after outer and inner failures with the intended transaction manager.

questions.question: How does REQUIRED propagation behave?
questions.answer: It joins an existing compatible transaction or starts one when absent, so several logical scopes can share one physical transaction.

questions.question: When is REQUIRES_NEW appropriate?
questions.answer: When an independent commit is a genuine requirement. It suspends the outer transaction and may need another connection; use it deliberately.

questions.question: How does NESTED differ from REQUIRES_NEW?
questions.answer: Where supported, NESTED uses savepoints within the same physical transaction; REQUIRES_NEW uses an independent transaction with independent completion.

questions.question: Why can REQUIRES_NEW exhaust a connection pool?
questions.answer: Threads can retain outer connections while waiting for inner transactions to obtain additional connections, creating capacity starvation.

questions.question: How would you choose propagation for audit records?
questions.answer: Decide whether audit data must survive business rollback, then test independent commit requirements, pool capacity and whether sensitive business state is exposed prematurely.

groups.title: Isolation and locking
groups.mechanism: Isolation governs observable concurrent database behavior, not arbitrary remote effects. The database's actual implementation and constraints determine which anomalies remain possible.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger isolation can simplify reasoning while increasing retries or blocking.
groups.verify: Run two controlled connections against the target database and assert the business invariant.

questions.question: What is transaction isolation?
questions.answer: A contract describing how concurrent transactions interact with uncommitted and changing data under the selected database implementation.

questions.question: When should a database constraint replace an application pre-check?
questions.answer: When uniqueness or another enforceable invariant must survive concurrent requests. A pre-check alone leaves a race before insertion or update.

questions.question: Does readOnly=true prohibit every write?
questions.answer: It is generally a hint and optimization signal whose enforcement depends on manager and database configuration; do not use it as authorization.

questions.question: Why can two individually valid reads lead to overselling?
questions.answer: Both transactions can decide from the same stale availability. Use an atomic conditional update, locking or appropriate isolation plus constraints.

questions.question: How would you make serialization retries safe?
questions.answer: Retry the whole transaction under a bounded policy, recomputing from fresh state and excluding irreversible external effects from repeated work.

groups.title: MVC request lifecycle
groups.mechanism: DispatcherServlet routes requests through mappings, adapters, argument resolution and response handling. Filters and handler interceptors belong to different pipeline layers.
groups.tradeOff: Centralized binding is convenient but error paths can bypass controller business code.
groups.verify: Test unmatched routes, malformed bodies and validation failures as well as successful controller invocation.

questions.question: What role does DispatcherServlet play?
questions.answer: It acts as Spring MVC's front controller, dispatching requests to appropriate handlers and coordinating result rendering or response writing.

questions.question: When should a servlet Filter be used instead of HandlerInterceptor?
questions.answer: Use filters for container-level request and response concerns; interceptors provide MVC handler-oriented integration and are not universal replacements for security filters.

questions.question: How are controller arguments resolved?
questions.answer: Configured argument resolvers bind route, query, header, body and contextual values, applying conversion and validation according to the parameter contract.

questions.question: Why can invalid JSON bypass a controller's try-catch block?
questions.answer: Deserialization can fail during argument resolution before the controller method is invoked; handle it through the appropriate global exception mechanism.

questions.question: How would you preserve an HTTP contract during controller refactoring?
questions.answer: Replay representative requests and compare statuses, media types, headers, field names and safe error bodies, including all binding and absence cases.

groups.title: Validation and conversion
groups.mechanism: Validation checks invariants after values are represented; conversion and binding can fail earlier. Method validation also depends on configured infrastructure and eligible invocation paths.
groups.tradeOff: Layered validation improves clarity but duplicate inconsistent rules create divergent behavior.
groups.verify: Test null, blank, malformed and cross-field invalid inputs at each supported entry point.

questions.question: How do binding and validation differ?
questions.answer: Binding maps external inputs into typed values; validation checks whether those values satisfy constraints. Either phase can fail independently.

questions.question: When is Valid needed for nested object validation?
questions.answer: When the validation contract should cascade into a nested value rather than checking only constraints on the containing object's fields.

questions.question: Why is NotNull insufficient for a required textual value?
questions.answer: It allows empty and whitespace-only strings. Choose constraints matching the business definition and normalize only where the contract permits.

questions.question: Why can method validation differ between direct and proxied calls?
questions.answer: Configured proxy-based method validation applies through eligible managed invocation paths, while direct construction or self-invocation can bypass that infrastructure.

questions.question: How would you validate a request used by both HTTP and message consumers?
questions.answer: Share domain invariants in a reusable boundary model or service contract, while keeping transport parsing and transport-specific error mapping separate.

groups.title: Error contracts
groups.mechanism: Exception resolution translates application and framework failures into client-visible outcomes. Safe diagnostics preserve useful context without leaking internal details.
groups.tradeOff: Uniform error shapes help clients, but distinct failure categories must remain distinguishable.
groups.verify: Assert stable codes and correlation identifiers for malformed, forbidden, missing and unavailable outcomes.

questions.question: What does ControllerAdvice provide?
questions.answer: Shared controller-related advice, including exception handling and binding customization across selected controllers.

questions.question: When should a domain error become a client error response?
questions.answer: When the client violated a documented request or business precondition; infrastructure outages should not be mislabeled as invalid input.

questions.question: How can ProblemDetail improve an API?
questions.answer: It supplies a standard structured problem representation, while the application still defines stable types, codes and safe detail content.

questions.question: Why is returning exception.getMessage directly risky?
questions.answer: Messages can expose SQL, infrastructure names, secrets or unstable implementation wording and make the public contract inconsistent.

questions.question: How would you distinguish a timeout from a confirmed failed write?
questions.answer: Report an unknown or pending outcome when commitment is uncertain, include an operation identity and provide a reconciliation path instead of inventing certainty.

groups.title: WebFlux and reactive context
groups.mechanism: WebFlux uses reactive execution with nonblocking components; returning a publisher does not change blocking libraries. Reactive context differs from ordinary thread-local storage.
groups.tradeOff: Reactive composition supports streaming and concurrency but requires careful demand and scheduler reasoning.
groups.verify: Inject slow dependencies, cancel subscriptions and inspect queueing, buffered memory and context continuity.

questions.question: How does WebFlux differ from Spring MVC?
questions.answer: They use different web execution models and integration stacks. Choose from workload, dependencies and team ownership rather than assuming one is universally faster.

questions.question: When must blocking JDBC work be isolated from an event loop?
questions.answer: Whenever that work would run on an event-loop thread. Use an intentional bounded boundary or an appropriate nonblocking driver and transaction model.

questions.question: What is Reactor Context used for?
questions.answer: Per-subscription contextual data that can travel through reactive composition, rather than relying on one stable executing thread.

questions.question: Why does calling block inside a reactive request path fail under load?
questions.answer: It can occupy scarce event-loop capacity or violate scheduler restrictions, preventing unrelated requests from progressing.

questions.question: How would you choose reactive code versus virtual-thread blocking code?
questions.answer: Compare streaming needs, library support, cancellation and operational complexity. Both need bounded access to finite downstream resources.

groups.title: HTTP clients
groups.mechanism: RestClient and WebClient serve different programming models. Transport configuration, timeout stages and pooled connection lifecycle remain explicit responsibilities.
groups.tradeOff: Connection reuse improves efficiency but stale connections and unbounded pending acquisition need control.
groups.verify: Fail DNS, connection establishment and response delivery separately; count actual downstream effects.

questions.question: When should RestClient be considered?
questions.answer: For a modern synchronous HTTP API in supported Spring versions, with explicit transport, error handling and timeout configuration.

questions.question: When is WebClient useful?
questions.answer: For reactive HTTP composition and streaming, especially when the rest of the execution model can remain nonblocking.

questions.question: Why are connect timeout and response timeout different?
questions.answer: One limits connection establishment; another limits waiting for response activity according to client semantics. Neither alone defines every end-to-end wait.

questions.question: Why can automatic retries duplicate a POST effect?
questions.answer: The remote server may commit before the client loses the response. Retry only with a safe operation contract such as durable idempotency.

questions.question: How would you prevent a client from exhausting the application under dependency failure?
questions.answer: Bound pending work, connection acquisition and total deadlines; classify retryable failures and expose capacity plus latency metrics.

groups.title: Events and scheduling
groups.mechanism: Application events coordinate in-process listeners; scheduling invokes local work. Neither automatically persists delivery or elects one worker across replicas.
groups.tradeOff: Simple local coordination is cheap but durable business work needs persistent identity and recovery.
groups.verify: Crash before and after a business effect, restart multiple replicas and verify duplicate-safe recovery.

questions.question: What is an application event in Spring?
questions.answer: A notification delivered through the application context's event infrastructure, with behavior influenced by listener and executor configuration.

questions.question: When is TransactionalEventListener useful?
questions.answer: When listener execution should align with a transaction phase. Its phase semantics do not by themselves provide durable cross-process delivery.

questions.question: How do fixed-delay and fixed-rate scheduling differ?
questions.answer: Fixed delay waits after an execution completes; fixed rate targets an invocation cadence. Asynchronous handoff changes what completion means.

questions.question: Why can a Scheduled task run more than once in a cluster?
questions.answer: Each application instance can schedule its own invocation. Local scheduling does not create cluster-wide uniqueness.

questions.question: How would you guarantee recoverable invoice-job execution?
questions.answer: Use durable job keys, atomic state transitions, bounded ownership and duplicate-safe effects, with storage-enforced fencing when stale workers must be rejected.

groups.title: Caching abstraction
groups.mechanism: Spring's cache annotations describe advice; the selected provider supplies storage, expiry and synchronization behavior. Cache keys and invalidation timing are part of correctness.
groups.tradeOff: Caching lowers origin load while introducing staleness and consistency obligations.
groups.verify: Test tenant separation, concurrent misses, rollback and failed post-commit invalidation.

questions.question: What does Cacheable normally do?
questions.answer: It checks the selected cache for a generated key and can reuse a stored result rather than invoking the method, subject to configuration.

questions.question: How does CachePut differ from Cacheable?
questions.answer: CachePut is intended to invoke the method and update the cache, while Cacheable can avoid method execution on a cache hit.

questions.question: Does sync=true imply distributed single-flight loading?
questions.answer: No universal cluster-wide guarantee follows. The selected cache provider determines its synchronization and loading capabilities.

questions.question: Why can self-invocation defeat cache annotations?
questions.answer: Ordinary Spring proxy advice is bypassed by direct target self-calls, so the expected cache interception may never run.

questions.question: How would you choose an invalidation strategy for mutable data?
questions.answer: Define allowed staleness, coordinate with successful commit, handle invalidation failure and prevent stale concurrent loaders from repopulating obsolete values.

groups.title: Testing Spring boundaries
groups.mechanism: Unit tests verify ordinary decisions; context, web and infrastructure tests verify the relevant framework contracts. Shared cached contexts must not conceal mutable global test state.
groups.tradeOff: Narrow tests give fast feedback while full integration tests expose wiring and real resource behavior.
groups.verify: Run representative tests alone and in parallel, including cleanup after a failing operation.

questions.question: What is the role of Spring TestContext?
questions.answer: It integrates context management and testing support with supported test frameworks, including context caching and configured test listeners.

questions.question: When should MockMvc be used?
questions.answer: To exercise Spring MVC request handling without requiring a full external HTTP deployment, while understanding which container and network behaviors remain outside scope.

questions.question: What does a transactional test rollback establish?
questions.answer: It rolls back work participating in that test-managed transaction; separately executed requests or asynchronous work may use different transactions.

questions.question: Why can a passing mock-based test miss a transaction bug?
questions.answer: A mock does not reproduce real commits, locks, constraints or transaction participation and can accept invalid call sequences.

questions.question: How would you verify proxy-based behavior independently of business logic?
questions.answer: Obtain the actual managed bean, exercise external and self-call paths, and assert observable transaction, cache or retry effects against a real supported boundary.

groups.title: Resources and application integration
groups.mechanism: Spring resource abstractions unify access to different locations without promising identical capabilities. Classpath content inside an archive may not be a normal filesystem file.
groups.tradeOff: Abstraction improves portability, but callers must respect stream ownership and location-specific limits.
groups.verify: Run from an executable archive, close streams and test missing or oversized resources.

questions.question: What does Resource abstract?
questions.answer: A handle to content such as classpath, filesystem or URL-backed data, with capabilities depending on the concrete resource implementation.

questions.question: When should getInputStream be preferred to getFile?
questions.answer: When content may be packaged inside an archive or otherwise lack a normal filesystem path; process the stream under explicit ownership.

questions.question: How does MessageSource support localization?
questions.answer: It resolves message keys and parameters for a locale; stable business decisions should use codes rather than translated display text.

questions.question: Why can a resource path become a security boundary?
questions.answer: Untrusted paths or URLs can access unintended files or destinations. Validate allowed locations and avoid treating arbitrary input as trusted resource configuration.

questions.question: How would you design a reusable Spring integration module?
questions.answer: Expose focused configuration and stable interfaces, avoid hidden global state, document lifecycle and conditional behavior, and test supported contexts and version combinations.

groups.title: @Component and @ComponentScan internals
groups.mechanism: Configuration processing discovers eligible annotated metadata and registers BeanDefinitions. Object construction happens later; a stereotype does not itself instantiate a service or open a transaction.
groups.tradeOff: Broad scanning saves configuration but can register unintended application or test components.
groups.verify: Inspect definitions before instantiation and start with an intentionally excluded package.

questions.question: How does @Component become a managed bean internally?
questions.answer: A configured scanner recognizes its metadata or composed stereotypes and registers a BeanDefinition, which the container later uses for construction and lifecycle processing.

questions.question: How do @Service and @Repository differ from @Component?
questions.answer: They are specialized stereotypes. Repository also participates in configured persistence exception translation; Service does not automatically make methods transactional.

questions.question: What does @ComponentScan actually control?
questions.answer: Candidate discovery within configured packages and filters, rather than every possible bean registered through imports or factory methods.

questions.question: Why can a correctly annotated @Service remain missing?
questions.answer: Its package may be outside scanning, excluded by filters or ineligible under conditions; the annotation alone does not register it globally.

questions.question: How would you audit a broad component scan?
questions.answer: List registered definitions and origins, identify accidental test or library components and replace unstable package assumptions with deliberate boundaries.

groups.title: @Autowired resolution internals
groups.mechanism: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor handles supported annotated injection metadata, while bean-factory dependency resolution chooses eligible candidates. Constructors, fields and methods have different initialization implications.
groups.tradeOff: Implicit resolution is convenient but ambiguous dependencies should have explicit roles.
groups.verify: Start contexts with zero, one and multiple candidates and assert injected identities.

questions.question: Which infrastructure interprets @Autowired?
questions.answer: Spring's configured injection post-processing and bean-factory resolution infrastructure; an ordinary object constructed outside that path receives no automatic injection.

questions.question: When can a constructor omit @Autowired?
questions.answer: A single constructor can generally be used implicitly; candidate resolution and required collaborator availability still apply.

questions.question: How do @Qualifier and @Primary influence @Autowired?
questions.answer: Qualifiers constrain the candidate role; Primary can prefer one eligible candidate for a single-valued dependency without removing other beans.

questions.question: Why can field injection hide an invalid object state?
questions.answer: The constructor can complete before required fields are supplied, and direct unit construction can leave those fields unset.

questions.question: How would you diagnose an ambiguous @Autowired dependency?
questions.answer: Inspect all matching definitions, qualifiers and primary markers, then express the intended role instead of relying on incidental naming or registration order.

groups.title: @Configuration, @Bean and @Import internals
groups.mechanism: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor participates in parsing configuration and registering definitions. Full configuration can be enhanced to intercept Bean method self-calls; lite mode behaves differently.
groups.tradeOff: Disabling enhancement reduces proxy requirements but ordinary inter-method calls may allocate duplicates.
groups.verify: Compare instance identities when invoking one Bean method from another with enhancement enabled and disabled.

questions.question: What processes @Configuration and @Bean declarations?
questions.answer: Spring's configuration-class infrastructure parses the metadata and registers bean definitions before ordinary bean creation.

questions.question: How does @Import differ from component scanning?
questions.answer: It explicitly brings configuration or supported import mechanisms into the configuration graph rather than discovering arbitrary candidate classes by package.

questions.question: What does proxyBeanMethods=false change internally?
questions.answer: The configuration class is not enhanced for Bean self-call interception, so direct method calls use ordinary Java execution.

questions.question: Why can a direct @Bean method call create a second connection pool?
questions.answer: In lite mode or an unmanaged configuration instance, the method can construct a fresh object instead of resolving the shared managed bean.

questions.question: How would you avoid inter-bean factory-call ambiguity?
questions.answer: Inject required collaborators as Bean method parameters and test creation count plus destruction ownership.

groups.title: @Profile, @Conditional and @Lazy internals
groups.mechanism: Conditions determine eligibility during configuration processing or registration. Lazy changes initialization or introduces deferred lookup at supported injection points; neither validates the eventual collaborator automatically.
groups.tradeOff: Deferral improves startup selectivity while moving some failures onto later use.
groups.verify: Evaluate supported profiles and force first use of every required lazy dependency.

questions.question: How is @Profile implemented conceptually?
questions.answer: It is a conditional configuration mechanism based on the active Environment profiles, influencing which definitions become eligible.

questions.question: When does @Conditional affect a bean?
questions.answer: At supported configuration evaluation phases, before the corresponding definition is used as an ordinary created bean; exact phase depends on the condition.

questions.question: How can @Lazy at an injection point defer resolution?
questions.answer: A supported lazy-resolution proxy can postpone obtaining the target until use, which differs from merely marking a definition for lazy initialization.

questions.question: Why does @Lazy not prove a circular dependency is solved?
questions.answer: The first invocation can traverse the same cycle or reveal missing wiring; construction deferral is not architectural decoupling.

questions.question: How would you test conditional annotation behavior?
questions.answer: Vary environment and available collaborators in isolated contexts, assert definition eligibility and invoke deferred paths explicitly.

groups.title: @Aspect, @Around and @Order internals
groups.mechanism: AspectJ-style annotation metadata can be translated into advisors applied by Spring's auto-proxy infrastructure. Around advice owns whether and when execution proceeds.
groups.tradeOff: Powerful interception can hide control flow and alter transaction or retry semantics.
groups.verify: Assert advice order, invocation count and failure propagation on the managed proxy.

questions.question: Does @Aspect alone register an object as a Spring bean?
questions.answer: No. It marks aspect metadata; the aspect still needs registration and the relevant AOP infrastructure enabled.

questions.question: How does @Around influence method execution?
questions.answer: Its advice can invoke the proceeding join point, change returned results or throw, so omitting proceed can skip the underlying operation.

questions.question: What does @Order affect for aspects?
questions.answer: It can influence advisor precedence under the supported ordering rules; nesting means entry and exit observations can occur in different directions.

questions.question: Why can an @Around timing metric undercount retries?
questions.answer: Its placement may wrap one attempt rather than the whole retrying operation, or vice versa; the measured boundary must be explicit.

questions.question: How would you prove an aspect is applied correctly?
questions.answer: Call through the actual proxy, include self-invocation and exception cases and assert observable outcomes rather than only checking annotation presence.

groups.title: @Transactional interceptor internals
groups.mechanism: Transaction metadata is read for eligible methods and used by transaction advice to select a manager, begin or join work and apply completion rules. Proxy reachability remains essential.
groups.tradeOff: Declarative boundaries reduce boilerplate while obscuring which resource and invocation actually participate.
groups.verify: Observe connection/transaction identity through external and internal calls with forced rollback.

questions.question: How does @Transactional cause database behavior internally?
questions.answer: Configured transaction advice reads its attributes and delegates to a transaction manager around an eligible invocation, controlling participation and completion.

questions.question: What does rollbackFor change?
questions.answer: It adjusts exception-based rollback rules; it does not undo external side effects or guarantee the exception crosses the advised boundary.

questions.question: How do class-level and method-level transaction declarations interact?
questions.answer: Method-specific metadata can refine applicable class defaults under Spring's resolution rules; verify the effective public use-case boundary.

questions.question: Why does @Transactional fail on a manually constructed service?
questions.answer: The object has not received the configured transaction interception infrastructure, so the annotation is only metadata.

questions.question: How would you test transaction advice ordering with retries?
questions.answer: Record transaction identity and committed rows for each attempt, then ensure the chosen nesting provides the intended fresh or shared transaction semantics.

groups.title: @RequestMapping and composed web annotations
groups.mechanism: Request-mapping infrastructure discovers controller handler metadata and selects a handler by route conditions. Argument resolvers and message converters execute before or after the method as appropriate.
groups.tradeOff: Composed annotations improve readability while overlapping mappings can become ambiguous.
groups.verify: Test method, path, media type, headers and malformed request behavior.

questions.question: How does @GetMapping work internally?
questions.answer: It is a composed RequestMapping declaration restricting HTTP method to GET; MVC handler-mapping infrastructure registers and matches the resulting metadata.

questions.question: How does @RestController differ from @Controller?
questions.answer: It composes controller detection with response-body semantics, causing supported return values to be written through response conversion rather than ordinary view naming.

questions.question: What interprets @RequestBody?
questions.answer: A configured argument resolver reads the request body through supported message converters before method invocation.

questions.question: Why can two @RequestMapping methods cause an ambiguity?
questions.answer: Their applicable route conditions can overlap without a uniquely selectable handler, during registration or request matching depending on the mappings.

questions.question: How would you migrate controller annotations safely?
questions.answer: Compare routing, binding, validation, response conversion and exception outcomes using actual HTTP contract fixtures.

groups.title: @Valid and @Validated boundaries
groups.mechanism: Valid requests cascaded Bean Validation, while Validated supplies Spring validation integration and group selection in supported paths. MVC's built-in method validation and proxy-based service validation have different activation rules.
groups.tradeOff: Annotation convenience can conceal missing providers or bypassed invocation paths.
groups.verify: Test nested invalid data and service calls both directly and through configured validation infrastructure.

questions.question: How does @Valid trigger nested validation?
questions.answer: At a supported validation boundary it requests cascading into the annotated value, using the installed Bean Validation provider and applicable constraints.

questions.question: What additional role can @Validated play?
questions.answer: It supports Spring's validation integration and validation-group selection, including configured method-validation use cases.

questions.question: Why does @NotNull accept an empty string?
questions.answer: It constrains nullness only; blank-text and size rules require appropriate separate constraints.

questions.question: Why can validation fail before a controller method executes?
questions.answer: Binding or validation infrastructure can reject arguments during resolution, so controller-local try-catch code is never reached.

questions.question: How would you verify annotation-driven validation actually runs?
questions.answer: Supply boundary-invalid values through each public entry path and assert real rejection plus safe errors, not just that the DTO carries constraints.

groups.title: @Async and @Scheduled execution internals
groups.mechanism: Configured post-processors detect eligible asynchronous and scheduled methods and integrate them with executors or schedulers. Submission and durable business completion are different events.
groups.tradeOff: Offloading improves responsiveness while requiring context, admission and error ownership.
groups.verify: Saturate executors, fail task bodies and terminate while accepted work remains.

questions.question: What activates @Async behavior?
questions.answer: Supported async infrastructure, commonly enabled through EnableAsync, applies advice that submits eligible managed invocations to the selected executor.

questions.question: Why does self-invocation bypass normal @Async advice?
questions.answer: The target calls itself without crossing the configured proxy, so the invocation can execute synchronously.

questions.question: What does @EnableScheduling contribute?
questions.answer: It activates scheduling infrastructure that detects supported Scheduled methods and registers local scheduling tasks.

questions.question: Why does a void @Async failure need special handling?
questions.answer: The caller has no returned Future to observe; configure an appropriate uncaught-exception reporting path and operational visibility.

questions.question: How would you make annotated background work reliable?
questions.answer: Bound executor admission, propagate approved context, record durable job identity where required and test cancellation, restart and cluster duplication.

groups.title: @Cacheable and cache-advisor internals
groups.mechanism: Caching advice evaluates cache metadata and keys around eligible method calls; a cache manager and provider implement storage behavior. Condition, unless and result timing have distinct roles.
groups.tradeOff: Annotation-based reuse is concise but incorrect keys or invalidation timing can violate data isolation.
groups.verify: Test tenant-specific inputs, self-calls, misses and updates that roll back.

questions.question: What interprets @Cacheable at runtime?
questions.answer: Configured caching advisors/interceptors use cache-operation metadata, resolve caches and keys, and decide whether the underlying method needs execution.

questions.question: How do condition and unless differ conceptually?
questions.answer: A condition can decide whether caching applies before invocation; unless can veto storing a result after evaluation, under the supported annotation contract.

questions.question: Why is @CacheEvict not automatically a distributed transaction?
questions.answer: Cache invalidation and database commit are separate resource operations whose ordering and failure behavior require explicit coordination.

questions.question: Why can @Cacheable return another tenant's value?
questions.answer: The key can omit tenant or authorization-relevant inputs, allowing distinct requests to reuse the same cached result.

questions.question: How would you verify a cache annotation migration?
questions.answer: Assert exact keys, actual invocation counts and provider behavior across rollback, concurrent loads and invalidation failures.
